Synthesize the hope for the Son of David found in Chronicles.

BIB.9.1.2.t: Identify Solomon as the wise king who built the Temple.
Name Elijah as the prophet who went up to heaven.
Recall that the kingdom broke into two pieces.
Observe that bad kings made the people worship idols.
Summarize the story of Elijah on Mount Carmel.
Compare the Northern Kingdom (Israel) and Southern Kingdom (Judah).
Categorize kings as 'Good' (like Hezekiah) or 'Bad' (like Ahab).
Analyze the ministry of Elijah and Elisha (miracles and confrontation).
Interpret the fall of Samaria (722 BC) and Jerusalem (586 BC).
Connect the reforms of Josiah to the Book of the Law.
Explain the sin of Jeroboam (golden calves).
Construct a synchronized timeline of the divided monarchy.
Evaluate the role of the prophet vis-à-vis the king.
Defend the justice of the Exile based on covenant curses.
Produce a study on the contest between Yahweh and Baal.

BIB.9.1.3.t: Identify Samuel as the boy who heard God call him.
Recall that Saul was the first king, but David was the best king.
Observe that David loved God with all his heart.
Summarize the transition from Judges to Kings.
Explain why God chose David (looks at the heart).
Compare Saul's disobedience with David's repentance.
Apply the lesson of friendship between David and Jonathan.
Analyze the Davidic Covenant in 2 Samuel 7.
Interpret the fall of the Ark of the Covenant.
Connect David's sin with Bathsheba to the turmoil in his family.
Explain the political unification of the tribes under David.
Construct a contrast between theocratic rule and monarchical rule.
Evaluate the character of Absalom and his rebellion.
Perform research on the historiography of the 'Court History of David'.
Synthesize the messianic themes in the Song of Hannah and David's Last Words.

BIB.9.1.4.t: Identify Esther as a Jewish queen.
Name Mordecai as her wise cousin.
Recall that she was brave to talk to the king.
Observe that God saved His people from bad Haman.
Explain the plot to destroy the Jews.
Compare the pride of Haman with the honor of Mordecai.
Apply the phrase 'For such a time as this'.
Analyze the fact that God's name is not mentioned in the book.
Connect the story to the providence of God.
Explain the vulnerability of Jews in the diaspora.
Construct an argument for the book's canonicity.
Evaluate the moral complexity of Esther's marriage to a pagan king.
Defend the doctrine of Providence using Esther as a case study.
Produce an essay on anti-semitism in the ancient world.

BIB.9.1.5.t: Identify Ezra as a teacher of God's Word.
Name the Temple as what they built again.
Recall that the people came back home from Babylon.
Observe that they were happy to read the Bible again.
Summarize the decree of Cyrus allowing the return.
Explain the opposition to building the Temple.
Compare the first return (Zerubbabel) and second return (Ezra).
Apply Ezra's example of studying and doing God's law.
Analyze the spiritual condition of the returnees.
Interpret the problem of intermarriage in Ezra.
Connect the rebuilding of the altar to true worship.
Explain the role of the scribe.
Construct a timeline of the Persian kings in Ezra.
Evaluate the exclusivity of the post-exilic community.
Defend the continuity of the covenant despite the lack of a king.
Synthesize the relationship between Ezra and Nehemiah.

BIB.9.1.6.t: Identify Joshua as the leader who fought the Battle of Jericho.
Name Rahab as the woman who helped the spies.
Recall that the walls fell down when they shouted.
Observe that God keeps His promises to give them the land.
Summarize the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho.
Compare the spies in Joshua 2 with the spies in Numbers 13.
Apply the verse 'Be strong and courageous'.
Analyze the three military campaigns (Central, Southern, Northern).
Connect the land allotment to the tribal promises.
Explain the concept of Herem (Holy War/Devoted to Destruction).
Construct a defense of the morality of the Canaanite conquest.
Evaluate the archaeological record of the destruction of Hazor.
Perform research on the Amarna Letters and the Habiru.
Synthesize the theme of 'Rest' in Joshua and the NT.

BIB.9.1.7.t: Name the Judges as leaders before there were kings.
Recall that the people forgot God many times.
Observe that God saved them when they prayed.
Summarize the cycle of Judges: Sin, Oppression, Repentance, Deliverance.
Explain how Gideon defeated the Midianites.
Compare the strength of Samson with his weakness for sin.
Analyze the refrain 'In those days there was no king in Israel'.
Interpret the tragic vow of Jephthah.
Connect the moral decline to the religious compromise.
Explain the role of the Holy Spirit coming upon the Judges.
Construct a chart of the Judges and their geographical areas.
Evaluate the disturbing ending of the book (civil war).
Defend the sovereignty of God in using flawed human instruments.
Produce an essay on the spiral of apostasy.

BIB.9.1.8.t: Identify Nehemiah as the cupbearer to the king.
Name the Wall of Jerusalem as what they built.
Recall that they worked with a tool in one hand and a sword in the other.
Observe that Nehemiah prayed before he acted.
Summarize how Nehemiah organized the people to build.
Explain why walls were important for a city.
Analyze the social justice issues Nehemiah addressed (usury).
Interpret the opposition of Sanballat and Tobiah.
Connect the reading of the Law to the renewal of the covenant.
Explain the significance of the city of Jerusalem.
Construct a profile of biblical leadership based on Nehemiah.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the reforms (did they last?).
Perform research on the topography of Jerusalem's walls.
Synthesize the theme of prayer and action in the book.

BIB.9.1.9.t: Identify Ruth as a loyal daughter-in-law.
Name Boaz as the kind man.
Recall that Ruth picked up grain in the fields.
Observe that King David came from Ruth's family.
Summarize the story of Naomi's return to Bethlehem.
Compare the choice of Orpah (left) and Ruth (stayed).
Apply the loyalty of Ruth to our friendships.
Analyze the literary structure of the book.
Interpret the significance of a Moabite in the line of Christ.
Connect the timeline of Ruth to the period of the Judges.
Construct a character study of Boaz as a type of Christ.
Evaluate the role of providence in the book (God is never named as acting directly).
Defend the inclusion of Gentiles in the plan of salvation.
Synthesize the book as a bridge between Judges and the Monarchy.

BIB.9.2.1.t: Identify Daniel as the man who prayed in the lions' den.
Recall that God rules over all kings.
Observe the writing on the wall.
Summarize the story of the fiery furnace.
Explain the dream of the statue made of metals.
Compare the pride of Nebuchadnezzar with the humility of Daniel.
Apply the courage to stand up for God.
Analyze the sovereignty of God over nations.
Interpret the vision of the four beasts.
Connect the 'Son of Man' to Jesus.
Explain the genre of Apocalyptic literature.
Construct a timeline of the 'Seventy Weeks' prophecy.
Evaluate the dating of Daniel (6th century vs. Maccabean).
Defend the supernatural prediction of future empires.
Produce a study on living faithfully in exile (Babylon).

BIB.9.2.2.t: Identify Ezekiel as the prophet with strange visions.
Name the Valley of Dry Bones.
Recall that God can make dead things alive.
Observe the vision of the wheels with eyes.
Summarize the vision of the Dry Bones coming to life.
Explain that God's glory left the temple because of sin.
Compare the heart of stone with the heart of flesh.
Categorize Ezekiel as a prophet during the Exile.
Analyze the symbolism of the watchman.
Interpret the vision of the New Temple.
Connect the phrase 'Then they will know that I am the Lord'.
Explain the individual responsibility for sin in Ezekiel 18.
Construct a diagram of the departure and return of God's glory.
Evaluate the apocalyptic imagery in the book.
Defend the regenerative work of the Spirit (Ezekiel 36).
Synthesize Ezekiel's temple vision with Revelation.

BIB.9.2.3.t: Identify Isaiah as a prophet who saw God on a throne.
Recall that he said Jesus would die for our sins.
Observe the vision of the wolf lying down with the lamb.
Summarize Isaiah's call (Here am I, send me).
Compare the judgment on idols with the comfort for Israel.
Categorize Isaiah as the most quoted prophet in the NT.
Analyze the two main sections: Judgment (1-39) and Comfort (40-66).
Connect the holiness of God to the need for cleansing.
Explain the historical context of the Assyrian invasion.
Construct a theology of the 'Holy One of Israel'.
Evaluate the critical theory of Deutero-Isaiah.
Defend the unity of the book.
Synthesize the vision of the New Heavens and New Earth.

BIB.9.2.4.t: Name the potter and the clay story.
Recall that he told people to stop sinning.
Observe that God promised a New Covenant.
Summarize Jeremiah's difficult job (no one listened).
Explain the New Covenant (law written on hearts).
Compare a true prophet with false prophets who said 'peace'.
Apply the lesson that obeying God is hard but right.
Analyze the acted parables (linen belt, potter's house).
Interpret the Temple Sermon (trusting rituals vs. obeying God).
Connect Jeremiah's suffering to the suffering of Jesus.
Explain the historical context of the fall of Jerusalem.
Construct a profile of Jeremiah's inner life and complaints.
Evaluate the promise of the New Covenant in Jeremiah 31.
Defend the justice of God's judgment on Judah.
Produce a study on the false prophets of Jeremiah's day.

BIB.9.3.10.t: Identify Obadiah as a short book.
Recall that we shouldn't laugh when others get hurt.
Observe that God defends His people.
Summarize the conflict between Jacob (Israel) and Esau (Edom).
Explain that pride brings people down.
Compare Edom's rocky fortress with God's power.
Analyze the historical background of Edom.
Interpret 'The day of the Lord is near for all nations'.
Connect the judgment of Edom to the protection of Zion.
Explain the lex talionis ('As you have done, it shall be done to you').
Construct a history of the Edomite/Israelite conflict.
Evaluate the sin of gloating over another's misfortune.
Defend God's justice in judging nations.
Synthesize the theme of the Kingdom belonging to the Lord.

BIB.9.3.11.t: Identify Zechariah as a prophet with strange dreams.
Name the King coming on a donkey.
Recall that it is 'Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit'.
Observe that God cares about Jerusalem.
Summarize the prophecy of the King on a donkey (Palm Sunday).
Explain the vision of the lampstand and olive trees.
Compare the bad shepherds with the Good Shepherd.
Apply the promise of God's Spirit helping us.
Interpret the prophecy of the 30 pieces of silver.
Connect Zechariah to the rebuilding of the Temple.
Construct a list of Messianic prophecies in Zechariah.
Evaluate the apocalyptic imagery and its relation to Revelation.
Defend the unity of the book (chapters 1-8 and 9-14).
Synthesize the theme of the piercing of the Messiah.

BIB.9.3.12.t: Recall that God sings over His people.
Observe that God will clean up the world.
Summarize the warning of judgment on the whole earth.
Explain the 'remnant' (the people who stay faithful).
Compare the bad day for enemies with the glad day for God's people.
Apply the verse 'He will quiet you with His love'.
Analyze the de-creation language in Zephaniah 1.
Interpret the call to seek righteousness and humility.
Connect Zephaniah to the reign of Josiah.
Explain the image of God as a singing warrior.
Construct a study on the 'Day of the Lord' theme.
Evaluate the syncretism (mixing religions) condemned in the book.
Defend the necessity of judgment for true restoration.
Synthesize the joy of restoration in Zephaniah 3.

BIB.9.3.1.t: Name justice as being fair to everyone.
Recall that God wants us to help the poor.
Observe that God sees how we treat others.
Summarize Amos' warnings to the rich people.
Explain 'Let justice roll down like waters'.
Compare religious singing with real obedience.
Apply the lesson of caring for the needy.
Analyze the judgment on the nations in chapters 1-2.
Interpret the vision of the plumb line.
Connect social justice to true worship.
Construct a theology of social justice based on Amos.
Evaluate the economic prosperity vs. moral decay of Israel.
Defend the importance of righteousness in society.
Produce an essay on the danger of religious hypocrisy.

BIB.9.3.2.t: Identify Habakkuk as a man who asked God questions.
Name the watchtower where he waited.
Recall 'The righteous shall live by faith'.
Observe that we can rejoice even when things are hard.
Summarize Habakkuk's questions (Why do bad people win?).
Explain God's answer (He is using the Babylonians).
Apply the choice to rejoice in God no matter what (Habakkuk 3).
Analyze the dialogue between the prophet and God.
Interpret 'The just shall live by his faith'.
Connect Habakkuk to the coming Babylonian invasion.
Explain the woe oracles against the Chaldeans.
Construct a theological response to the problem of evil based on Habakkuk.
Evaluate Paul's use of Habakkuk 2:4 in Romans and Galatians.
Defend the sovereignty of God in using wicked nations.
Produce a reflection on finding joy in God alone.

BIB.9.3.3.t: Identify Haggai as a prophet after the exile.
Name the Temple as what needed building.
Recall that the people were building their own houses instead.
Observe that God wants to be first.
Explain why the people stopped building (discouragement).
Compare the small new temple with the glorious old one.
Apply the lesson of putting God's work first.
Analyze the connection between spiritual obedience and physical blessing.
Interpret the prophecy that the glory of the latter house will be greater.
Connect Haggai to Zerubbabel and Joshua the Priest.
Explain the 'shaking of the heavens and earth'.
Construct a timeline of the post-exilic period (Ezra/Haggai).
Evaluate the messianic significance of the signet ring.
Defend the importance of the visible church/temple.
Produce an essay on overcoming spiritual apathy.

BIB.9.3.4.t: Identify Hosea as the man who married Gomer.
Name God's love as a never-stopping love.
Recall that God forgives us when we run away.
Observe that God wants us to love Him back.
Summarize Hosea's marriage as a picture of God and Israel.
Compare idolatry to cheating on a spouse.
Apply the call to return to the Lord.
Analyze the metaphor of spiritual adultery.
Interpret the names of Hosea's children (Not my people).
Connect Hosea's redemption of Gomer to Christ redeeming the church.
Explain the historical context of the Northern Kingdom.
Construct a theology of God's emotional engagement (jealousy/love).
Evaluate the shock value of the prophetic sign act.
Defend the relentless love of God ('Hesed').
Synthesize Hosea's message with the New Testament bride imagery.

BIB.9.3.5.t: Identify the locusts as bugs that ate everything.
Recall that God promised to pour out His Spirit.
Observe that we should pray when bad things happen.
Explain the promise of the Holy Spirit.
Compare a natural disaster with God's judgment.
Apply the call to rend hearts, not garments.
Analyze the concept of the 'Day of the Lord'.
Interpret the prophecy of the Spirit quoted in Acts 2.
Connect the locust plague to future judgment.
Explain the call to national repentance.
Construct a timeline of the fulfillment of Joel 2.
Evaluate the use of Joel in Peter's Pentecost sermon.
Defend the necessity of repentance for restoration.
Synthesize the theme of judgment and blessing.

BIB.9.3.6.t: Identify Jonah as the man swallowed by a big fish.
Name Nineveh as the city he didn't want to go to.
Recall that God loves people everywhere.
Observe that you can't run away from God.
Summarize the story of Jonah's running and preaching.
Explain why Jonah was angry (he hated the Assyrians).
Compare God's mercy with Jonah's anger.
Apply the lesson that God cares for our enemies.
Analyze Jonah's prayer from the fish.
Interpret the sign of Jonah mentioned by Jesus.
Connect the book to Israel's failure to be a light to the nations.
Explain the satire and irony in the book.
Construct a profile of the Assyrian cruelty to understand Jonah's reluctance.
Evaluate the ending of the book (the unanswered question).
Defend the historicity of the book against 'parable' views.
Synthesize the missionary heart of God in the OT.

BIB.9.3.7.t: Identify Malachi as the last book of the Old Testament.
Recall that the people were robbing God.
Observe that God promised to send Elijah before the end.
Summarize the disputes between God and the people.
Explain the prophecy of the messenger (John the Baptist).
Compare true worship with bored worship.
Apply the teaching on tithes and offerings.
Analyze the question-and-answer style of the book.
Interpret 'I have loved Jacob but hated Esau'.
Connect the 'Sun of Righteousness' to Jesus.
Explain the problem of divorce and intermarriage in Malachi.
Construct a profile of the spiritual lethargy of the post-exilic community.
Evaluate the prophecy of Elijah and its fulfillment in John the Baptist.
Defend the immutability of God ('I the Lord do not change').
Synthesize the end of the OT and the 400 years of silence.

BIB.9.3.8.t: Name Bethlehem as the place a Ruler would come from.
Recall that God wants us to be kind and humble.
Summarize Micah 6:8 (Act justly, love mercy, walk humbly).
Explain the prophecy about Jesus' birth.
Compare false rulers with the Good Shepherd.
Apply the call to walk humbly with God.
Analyze the lawsuit motif in the book.
Interpret the prophecy of the mountain of the Lord.
Connect Micah's message to his contemporary, Isaiah.
Explain the imagery of casting sins into the sea.
Construct a theology of what God requires of man.
Defend the consistency of justice and mercy in God's character.
Produce a reflection on 'Who is a God like you?'

BIB.9.3.9.t: Identify Nahum as a prophet against a bad city.
Recall that God is slow to anger but strong.
Observe that God protects those who trust Him.
Explain that Nineveh went back to being bad after Jonah.
Compare God as a stronghold with God as a flood.
Apply the truth that God judges evil.
Analyze the poetic description of the siege of Nineveh.
Interpret the character of God in Nahum 1.
Connect the fall of Nineveh to historical records.
Explain why God's patience eventually ends.
Construct a comparison of Jonah (mercy) and Nahum (judgment).
Evaluate the moral necessity of divine wrath against cruelty.
Defend the justice of God in history.
Synthesize the comfort Nahum brings to God's oppressed people.

BIB.9.4.1.t: Identify Deuteronomy as Moses' last speech.
Name the command to love God with all our heart.
Observe that God wants us to remember His laws.
Compare the blessings for obeying and the curses for disobeying.
Apply the command to teach God's word to children.
Analyze the structure of the book as a Suzerain-Vassal treaty.
Interpret the requirement for the future King.
Connect Deuteronomy to Jesus' temptation (He quoted it 3 times).
Explain the significance of Moses' death on Mt. Nebo.
Construct a theology of the 'heart' in Deuteronomy.
Defend the unity of the Law.
Produce an essay on how Deuteronomy serves as the theological center of the OT.

BIB.9.4.2.t: Identify Exodus as the book about leaving Egypt.
Name Moses as the leader God chose.
Recall the crossing of the Red Sea.
Observe the Ten Commandments as God's rules.
Summarize the ten plagues and the Passover.
Compare the slavery in Egypt to freedom in the wilderness.
Apply the lesson that God rescues His people.
Analyze the structure: Deliverance (1-18), Covenant (19-24), Tabernacle (25-40).
Interpret the significance of the Divine Name (Yahweh/I AM).
Connect the Passover Lamb to Christ.
Explain the purpose of the Tabernacle dwelling.
Construct a map of the possible routes of the Exodus.
Evaluate the date of the Exodus (Early vs. Late date).
Defend the historicity of the event against minimalist claims.
Produce an essay on Exodus as the paradigm for salvation in the Bible.

BIB.9.4.3.t: Identify Genesis as the book of 'Beginnings'.
Name the first man and woman made by God.
Recall the story of Noah's Ark.
Observe that God made everything good.
Summarize the lives of the four Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph).
Explain the two main sections: Primeval History (1-11) and Patriarchal History (12-50).
Compare the creation account with the fall of man.
Categorize Genesis as the foundation for the rest of the Bible.
Analyze the structure of the 'Toledot' (generations) throughout the book.
Interpret the significance of the Abrahamic Covenant for world history.
Connect the 'seed of the woman' promise to the rest of the book.
Explain the theology of Election in the choice of Jacob over Esau.
Construct a defense of Mosaic authorship against the Documentary Hypothesis.
Evaluate the literary framework view of Genesis 1 versus literal creationism.
Perform research on the cultural background of patriarchal customs.
Synthesize the theme of God's sovereignty in the Joseph narrative.

BIB.9.4.4.t: Recall that we cannot keep all the rules perfectly.
Name Jesus as the one who kept the rules for us.
Observe that God forgives us when we fail.
Summarize how the Law shows us our sin.
Explain how the sacrifices show us God's grace.
Compare trying to be good with trusting in God.
Apply the idea that the Law is a guide for how to live, not how to be saved.
Analyze the Three Uses of the Law (Mirror, Restraint, Guide).
Interpret Paul's statement that the Law is a 'tutor' to lead us to Christ.
Connect the failure of Israel to keep the Law with the need for a New Covenant.
Explain how grace is present even in the Old Testament.
Construct a clear distinction between Law and Gospel hermeneutics.
Evaluate the error of legalism vs. antinomianism.
Defend the continuity of salvation by grace through faith in both Testaments.
Synthesize the Torah as a witness to Christ.

BIB.9.4.5.t: Identify Leviticus as a book about holiness.
Name the priests as helpers in God's house.
Recall that God wants His people to be clean.
Summarize the five main offerings (Burnt, Grain, Peace, Sin, Guilt).
Categorize the feasts of Israel found in Leviticus 23.
Analyze the Day of Atonement ceremony (Leviticus 16).
Interpret the call to 'Be holy, for I am holy.'
Connect the dietary laws to the idea of separation from the nations.
Explain the role of the Scapegoat.
Construct a theology of substitutionary atonement based on Leviticus.
Evaluate the relevance of the Holiness Code for New Testament believers.
Defend the necessity of blood sacrifice.
Synthesize the book of Leviticus with the book of Hebrews.

BIB.9.4.6.t: Identify Numbers as the book where they counted the people.
Name the 12 spies who went into the land.
Recall that the people complained a lot in the desert.
Observe the cloud that led them by day.
Summarize the rebellion at Kadesh Barnea.
Explain why they wandered for 40 years (one year for each day spied).
Compare the faith of Joshua and Caleb with the fear of the others.
Apply the story of the Bronze Serpent.
Analyze the layout of the camp with the Tabernacle in the center.
Interpret the story of Balaam and his donkey.
Connect the grumbling of Israel to the spiritual danger of discontent.
Explain the transition from the old generation to the new generation.
Construct a timeline of the wilderness wanderings.
Evaluate the character flaws of Moses that kept him from the Promised Land.
Perform research on the geography of the wilderness journey.
Synthesize the typology of the wilderness as the Christian life.

BIB.9.5.1.t: Identify that there is a time for everything.
Name the 'Preacher' who looked for happiness.
Recall that only God can make us truly happy.
Observe that toys break and don't last forever.
Summarize the search for meaning in pleasure, work, and wisdom.
Compare life 'under the sun' with life with God.
Apply the conclusion: Fear God and keep His commandments.
Analyze the reality of death and injustice in the book.
Interpret the call to remember the Creator in youth.
Connect Ecclesiastes to the dissatisfaction of materialism.
Explain the difference between fleeting joy and eternal purpose.
Construct a philosophical apologetic using Ecclesiastes.
Evaluate the authorship debate (Solomon vs. later sage).
Defend the book's presence in the canon as essential realism.
Produce a reflection on finding joy in the simple gifts of God.

BIB.9.5.2.t: Identify Job as a man who loved God but suffered.
Name God as the one who is in charge of everything.
Recall that Job did not stop loving God even when sad.
Observe that God made the Behemoth and Leviathan.
Summarize the test of Job (losing family and health).
Explain that bad things happen even to good people.
Compare Job's patience with his friends' bad advice.
Apply the truth that we should trust God even when we don't understand.
Analyze the dialogue between Job and his three friends.
Interpret God's answer from the whirlwind.
Connect the book to the problem of evil (Theodicy).
Explain the limit of Satan's power.
Construct a summary of the retribution principle and how Job refutes it.
Defend the sovereignty of God in suffering.
Synthesize Job as a type of the righteous sufferer (Christ).

BIB.9.5.3.t: Identify Proverbs as a book of wise sayings.
Name Solomon as the wisest king.
Recall that listening to parents is wise.
Observe the difference between a wise child and a foolish one.
Summarize the theme: The Fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
Explain the difference between knowledge and wisdom.
Compare the sluggard (lazy person) with the ant.
Apply proverbs about words and anger to daily life.
Analyze the structure: Father's instruction vs. Woman Wisdom.
Interpret the nature of a proverb (general truth, not absolute promise).
Connect wisdom to the order of creation.
Explain the warning against the 'Strange Woman' (Folly).
Construct a topical study of Proverbs (money, speech, friendship).
Evaluate the personification of Wisdom in chapter 8.
Defend the practical value of Proverbs for modern ethics.
Synthesize the 'Proverbs 31 Woman' as an ideal of wisdom.

BIB.9.5.4.t: Identify Psalms as songs to God.
Name David as a writer of songs.
Observe that we can sing when happy or sad.
Summarize the different types of Psalms (Praise, Thanksgiving, Lament).
Explain how to use Psalms for prayer.
Compare Psalm 1 (The Righteous) and Psalm 2 (The Messiah).
Apply a Psalm to your own feelings.
Analyze the structure of Hebrew poetry (Parallelism).
Connect the five books of Psalms to the Torah.
Explain the use of Selah and other musical terms.
Construct a theology of the emotions based on the Psalms.
Evaluate the imprecatory Psalms (prayers for judgment).
Defend the use of Psalms in corporate worship.
Produce a study on the Kingship of Yahweh in the Psalms.

BIB.9.5.5.t: Identify this book as a song about love.
Name marriage as a special gift from God.
Recall that God loves His people very much.
Observe that husband and wife are best friends.
Summarize it as a poem about a bride and groom.
Explain that marriage is between a man and a woman.
Compare the love in the book to God's love for the church.
Apply the idea of loyalty in relationships.
Analyze the poetic language of love and devotion.
Interpret the book as a celebration of marital intimacy.
Connect the marriage covenant to the biblical view of sexuality.
Construct a comparison of literal vs. allegorical interpretations.
Evaluate the biblical view of sexuality vs. cultural views.
Defend the holiness of physical intimacy within marriage.
Synthesize the Song with the 'Bride of Christ' imagery in the NT.

CFL.1.1.1.t: Recognize the three Greek accent marks by sight: the acute (´), the grave (`), and the circumflex (˜ or ῀).

greek: τίς (tis) — 'who?' vs. τις (tis) — 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Name which vowels in a written word carry an accent mark and read the word with stress on that syllable.

greek: τίς (tis) — 'who?' vs. τις (tis) — 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: State the rule that a Greek accent can stand only on one of the last three syllables (antepenult, penult, ultima).

greek: τίς (tis) — 'who?' vs. τις (tis) — 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Apply the rule that the acute may stand on any of the last three syllables, the circumflex only on the last two, and the grave only on the final syllable.

greek: τίς (tis) — 'who?' vs. τις (tis) — 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Explain how a final acute changes to a grave when another word follows without intervening punctuation.

greek: τίς (tis) — 'who?' vs. τις (tis) — 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Explain that Greek verb accent is recessive, moving as far back toward the antepenult as the length of the ultima allows, and predict a verb's accent placement.

CFL.1.1.3.t: Recite the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet in order by name (alpha, beta, gamma …).
Match each lowercase Greek letter to its uppercase form.
Write each Greek letter, both lowercase and uppercase, in correct handwritten form.
Give the basic consonant and vowel sound of each letter and read simple Greek syllables aloud.
Write the final form of sigma (ς) at the end of a word and the medial/initial sigma (σ) elsewhere.
Transliterate a Greek word into Roman letters, including gamma-nasal (γγ, γκ) as 'ng'/'nk'.
Read an unfamiliar Greek word aloud smoothly, combining letters, breathings, and accents at sight.

CFL.1.1.4.t: Name the seven Greek vowels (α, ε, η, ι, ο, υ, ω) and identify which are always long (η, ω) and which are always short (ε, ο).
Pronounce each vowel with its standard classroom (Erasmian) sound.
Recognize and pronounce the proper diphthongs (αι, ει, οι, υι, αυ, ευ, ου, ηυ) as single vowel sounds.
Identify the iota subscript (ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ) and explain that it marks an original long-vowel diphthong that is no longer pronounced.
Distinguish a genuine diphthong from two vowels pronounced separately when marked by a diaeresis (¨).
Explain how vowel length and diphthongs affect syllable quantity and thus accent placement.

CFL.1.2.1.t: Explain that Greek verb tenses convey kind of action (aspect), not only time.
Define punctiliar (undefined/simple) aspect and linear (ongoing, progressive) aspect.
Contrast the aorist as portraying an action as a whole with the imperfect as portraying an action as ongoing or repeated in past time.
Identify the present tense as expressing continuous or habitual action in a given passage.
Analyze how the perfect aspect presents a completed action with continuing results.
Interpret a New Testament verse where the aspectual choice carries exegetical or theological weight (e.g., ongoing vs. once-for-all action).

CFL.1.2.2.t: Look up a Greek word by its Strong's number in a concordance or lexicon.
Find a word's dictionary (lemma) form and read its glosses in a beginning lexicon.
Distinguish a word's range of meaning (semantic range) and select the sense that fits its context.
Explain and avoid the root fallacy, recognizing that a word's meaning comes from usage, not from the sum of its parts or etymology.
Use an advanced lexicon such as BDAG (New Testament) or Liddell-Scott (classical) to trace a word's attested usage.
Conduct a word study that weighs usage across the New Testament and the Septuagint to establish a word's meaning in a passage.

CFL.1.2.3.t: Recognize common Koine prepositions (ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό, πρός, διά, μετά, κατά, ὑπό, σύν) and give a basic gloss for each.

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό — common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: State which case each preposition governs and translate the prepositional phrase accordingly.

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό — common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: Explain how a preposition that takes more than one case shifts meaning with the case it governs (e.g., διά + genitive 'through' vs. διά + accusative 'because of').

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό — common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: Relate the spatial picture of a preposition to its case (e.g., genitive = motion from, dative = position in/at, accusative = motion toward).

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό — common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: Analyze a preposition's contribution to the meaning of a New Testament clause, including prepositions prefixed to verbs.

CFL.1.3.1.t: Recognize the Greek definite article and decline it for the masculine, feminine, and neuter in the nominative singular and plural (ὁ, ἡ, τό, οἱ, αἱ, τά).
Match an article to its noun by agreement in gender, number, and case.
Distinguish the attributive position (article–adjective–noun or article–noun–article–adjective), in which the adjective modifies the noun.
Distinguish the predicate position (adjective without a repeated article), in which the adjective asserts something about the noun.
Identify anarthrous (article-less) constructions and describe how the absence of the article affects meaning.
Evaluate a disputed anarthrous construction (e.g., the predicate nominative in John 1:1) using word order and the Colwell/Granville Sharp considerations.

CFL.1.3.2.t: Name the five Greek noun cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, and vocative.
State the basic syntactic function of each case (subject, of/possession, to/for/in, direct object, direct address).
Decline a first-declension and a second-declension noun fully in the singular and plural.
Decline a third-declension noun, accounting for stem changes in the nominative and dative plural.
Identify the case, number, and gender of a noun in a New Testament sentence and translate it by its function.
Distinguish nuanced case functions in exegesis (e.g., subjective vs. objective genitive; dative of means, place, or reference).

CFL.1.3.3.t: Recognize a Greek participle as a verbal adjective and identify its participial ending.
Parse a participle for tense, voice, gender, number, and case.
Distinguish adjectival participles (attributive and substantival) from adverbial (circumstantial) participles.
Translate an adverbial participle with the appropriate relation to the main verb (temporal, causal, concessive, conditional, means, or manner).
Identify and translate the genitive absolute construction.
Identify supplementary (complementary) participles that complete the idea of verbs such as παύομαι and ἄρχομαι.
Analyze how a participle's tense conveys aspect and its time relative to the main verb in a New Testament passage.

CFL.1.3.4.t: Identify the six principal Greek indicative tenses: present, imperfect, future, aorist, perfect, and pluperfect.
Conjugate a regular (ω-) verb in the present active indicative across all persons and numbers.
Conjugate a verb in the imperfect and future active indicative, recognizing the augment and the tense formatives.
Recognize the augment as the marker of past-time (secondary) tenses in the indicative.
Conjugate first (sigmatic) and second aorist active indicative verbs and tell them apart.
Conjugate the perfect and pluperfect active indicative, recognizing reduplication.
Parse any indicative verb from the New Testament by tense, voice, mood, person, and number.

CFL.1.3.5.t: Name the three Greek voices: active, middle, and passive.
Explain that active voice presents the subject as doing the action and passive voice as receiving it.
Describe the middle voice as presenting the subject as acting with reference to or upon itself, and translate simple middle forms.
Recognize deponent verbs, which are middle or passive in form but active in meaning, and translate them actively.
Distinguish middle from passive forms where they share endings, using context to decide the voice.
Evaluate the theological significance of voice in a passage (e.g., the divine passive as a reverent way of referring to God's action).

CFL.1.4.2.t: Use an interlinear Greek-English New Testament to locate the Greek word beneath its English gloss.
Look up an unfamiliar form in a parsing guide or analytical lexicon to find its dictionary form.
Consult a reference grammar to check a specific syntactic question rather than reading a whole translation from it.
Translate a clause first from the Greek text, then use an interlinear only to check the result, noting where over-dependence would have masked the grammar.
Evaluate the strengths and limits of interlinears, recognizing that their word-for-word English order distorts Greek syntax.
Demonstrate growing independence by reading and parsing a passage directly, reserving tools for confirmation.

CFL.1.4.3.t: Explain that the New Testament survives in many handwritten manuscripts that differ in small ways, producing textual variants.
Locate the critical apparatus at the foot of the page in a Greek New Testament (e.g., NA28 or UBS).
Read the basic sigla and abbreviations of the apparatus to identify a variant reading and the witnesses cited for it.
Compare two variant readings of a verse and state how each would affect translation or meaning.
Apply introductory canons of textual criticism, weighing external evidence (age and distribution of witnesses) and internal evidence (the reading that best explains the others).

CFL.2.1.1.t: Recognize that small marks appear above and below Hebrew words in a printed Hebrew Bible and that they help guide reading aloud
Identify cantillation (te'amim) marks as a system separate from the consonants and vowel points
Explain that cantillation marks serve three roles: musical chant, word stress (accent), and punctuation that groups words into phrases
Distinguish disjunctive from conjunctive accents and locate the major dividers such as silluq, atnach, and zaqef
Use the atnach to identify the main clausal division of a verse and discuss how that division can affect interpretation
Analyze a verse where the Masoretic accentuation supports or challenges a particular translation or theological reading

CFL.2.1.2.t: Recite the names of the 22 Hebrew consonants in order
Recognize and name each of the 22 consonantal letters by sight
Write each Hebrew consonant by hand in the square (Aramaic) script
Produce the standard consonantal sound value of each letter, including the gutturals aleph, he, chet, and ayin
Transliterate Hebrew consonants into Roman letters using a consistent academic scheme
Distinguish easily confused letter pairs such as bet/kaf, dalet/resh, he/chet, and vav/zayin in unpointed text
Compare academic and general-purpose transliteration systems and apply one consistently to a printed verse

CFL.2.1.3.t: Notice that a dot inside a Hebrew letter changes how some letters look

Identify the dagesh forte as a doubling of a consonant and read a word with a doubled letter
Read and classify the shewa as either vocal (a reduced vowel) or silent (a syllable closer)
Recognize the mappiq in final he and the meteg, and explain the pronunciation effect of each
Explain how a dagesh forte in doubling can signal grammatical information such as the Piel binyan or an assimilated nun

CFL.2.1.4.t: Recognize that some Hebrew letters take a different shape at the end of a word
Name the five letters that have a final (sofit) form: kaf, mem, nun, pe, and tsade
Match each final form to its ordinary medial form
Write the five final forms by hand and place them correctly at the end of a word
Read words containing final forms without mistaking a sofit letter for a different consonant

CFL.2.1.5.t: Recognize that small dots and dashes below and beside the consonants stand for vowels
Name the basic full vowels (qamets, patach, tsere, segol, chireq, cholem, qibbuts, shureq) and their sounds
Read a fully pointed Hebrew word by combining each consonant with its vowel
Distinguish long, short, and reduced (chateph) vowels and identify the chateph vowels under gutturals
Explain the difference between qamets gadol and qamets chatuph and read each correctly
Divide a pointed word into syllables and mark whether each syllable is open or closed

CFL.2.2.1.t: Recognize the letter vav prefixed to a word as the common word meaning 'and'
Translate the conjunction vav as 'and,' 'but,' 'or,' or 'now' according to context
Identify the vav-consecutive (vav plus a prefixed verb) as the signal of Hebrew narrative sequence
Distinguish the vav-consecutive (wayyiqtol) chain that carries a story forward from a simple conjunctive vav
Translate a wayyiqtol narrative chain into smooth English past-tense sequence
Analyze how a break in the wayyiqtol chain marks a scene shift, background information, or theological emphasis in a narrative

CFL.2.2.4.t: Recognize that a Hebrew verb can change its ending or its prefix to show a different form
Identify the perfect (qatal) conjugation by its suffixed person endings
Identify the imperfect (yiqtol) conjugation by its prefixed person markers
Explain the perfect as viewing action as complete and the imperfect as viewing action as incomplete
Translate perfect and imperfect verbs into appropriate English tenses using context rather than a fixed rule
Analyze how Hebrew verbal aspect, not tense, shapes the meaning of a chosen prophetic or poetic verse

CFL.2.2.5.t: Recognize that some short Hebrew words are attached to the front of another word
Identify the inseparable prepositions bet ('in/with'), kaf ('like/as'), and lamed ('to/for') as prefixed letters
Translate a word carrying a prefixed preposition, restoring the base word
Explain how a prefixed preposition merges with the definite article and changes its vowel
Parse a word that combines a prefixed preposition, an article, and a pronominal suffix

CFL.2.2.6.t: Recognize the common independent pronouns such as ani ('I'), atah ('you'), and hu ('he')
Identify the definite article ha- prefixed to a noun and explain that Hebrew has no indefinite article
Match independent personal pronouns to their person, gender, and number
Identify a pronominal suffix on a noun and translate it as a possessive (e.g., 'his,' 'their')
Identify a pronominal suffix on a verb or preposition and translate it as an object
Parse the doubling of the article's following consonant and the article's vowel changes before gutturals

CFL.2.2.8.t: Recognize that a Hebrew root can appear in several verb patterns with related meanings
Name the seven major binyanim (Qal, Niphal, Piel, Pual, Hiphil, Hophal, Hithpael)
Identify the Qal as the simple active stem and the Niphal as its common passive or reflexive
Explain the intensive Piel/Pual pair and the causative Hiphil/Hophal pair by voice and function
Recognize the reflexive Hithpael by its characteristic infixed tav
Parse a finite verb fully by stating its binyan, conjugation, person, gender, and number
Analyze how a change of binyan shifts the meaning of a root in a chosen verse

CFL.2.3.1.t: Look up the meaning of a Hebrew word using a glossary or interlinear tool
Conduct a basic word study by tracing how one Hebrew term is used across several passages
Explain the grammatical-historical method as reading a text according to its grammar, its author, and its original setting
Interpret a verse by combining word study, grammatical parsing, and its literary context
Synthesize the exegetical findings of several passages into a careful summary of a biblical theme
Distinguish sound exegesis (drawing meaning out of the text) from eisegesis (reading meaning into it) in a worked example

CFL.2.3.2.t: Recognize that a Hebrew lexicon lists words with their meanings and references
Locate a Hebrew word in a lexicon by its root or dictionary form
Read a lexicon entry and identify its glosses, grammatical notes, and cited passages
Explain that a word carries a semantic range and select the gloss that fits a given context
Compare the arrangement and information of BDB and HALOT and use each to research a word

Use a paradigm chart to match a suffix or prefix to its person, gender, and number
Parse regular (strong) verbs by comparing them to the Qal paradigm chart
Parse nouns and pronouns using reference charts for endings and suffixes
Parse weak verbs (I-nun, I-guttural, III-he, hollow) with the aid of morphology charts

CFL.2.3.4.t: Recognize that Hebrew continued to be used and studied in the centuries between the Old and New Testaments
Identify the Second Temple period and name key bodies of literature such as the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint
Explain how the Masoretes preserved and pointed the Hebrew text long after the biblical period
Describe the rise of rabbinic literature (Mishnah and Talmud) and its relationship to Mishnaic Hebrew
Discuss how Second Temple and rabbinic sources illuminate the language and background of the Old Testament

Identify poetic features such as imagery, repetition, and figurative language in a psalm
Analyze the poetic devices of a wisdom or prophetic passage and describe their effect on meaning

CFL.2.4.4.t: Recognize that Hebrew poems are built from pairs of matching lines

Identify climactic (stairstep) parallelism that repeats and builds across lines
Analyze the parallelism of a psalm and explain how the paired lines shape its meaning

CFL.2.4.5.t: Recognize that the same Hebrew verse can be rendered in more than one English wording
Distinguish a formal (literal, word-for-word) translation from a dynamic (thought-for-thought) translation
Compare two English versions of a verse and account for their differences from the Hebrew
Produce a literal working translation of a verse, then a smoother idiomatic rendering
Explain the special challenges of translating Hebrew poetry, including imagery and parallelism
Defend translation choices for a passage by appealing to grammar, semantic range, and context

CFL.2.4.6.t: Recognize the vav-consecutive verb form as the marker that keeps a Hebrew story moving
Identify the wayyiqtol chain that forms the backbone of Old Testament narrative
Explain how the narrative chain distinguishes the main storyline from background comments
Trace the sequence of events in a narrative by following its wayyiqtol verbs
Analyze how a shift in the narrative chain (a disruption or aside) carries theological weight in a chosen story

CFL.3.1.1.t: Identify who or what a sentence is about (the subject) and who or what receives the action (the object).
Point out small words that show relationship or position, such as 'to,' 'from,' 'with,' and 'in.'
Explain how English uses word order and prepositions to show a noun's job in a sentence.
Compare how a language with cases (such as Latin) changes a noun's ending to show its function, while English uses word order or a preposition instead.
Match common Latin or Greek cases (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative) to the English prepositions or roles that express the same idea.
Analyze how a single case can carry several functions and why translators must choose the right English preposition from context.
Evaluate the trade-offs between case-marking and prepositional systems, explaining what each gains in precision or flexibility.

CFL.3.1.2.t: Recognize that people around the world speak many different languages.
Identify that some languages look and sound similar because they are related, like members of a family.
Name major language families, such as Indo-European and Semitic, and give an example language in each.
Explain how linguists group languages into families using shared vocabulary, sound patterns, and grammar.
Trace how Latin, Greek, and the Germanic languages (including English) descend from a common Indo-European ancestor.
Compare features of the Semitic family (such as Hebrew's triconsonantal roots) with those of Indo-European languages.
Analyze cognate sets across related languages to infer their shared origin and reconstruct likely ancestral forms.

CFL.3.1.3.t: Learn that many English words come from older languages, especially Latin and Greek.
Identify a common root within a word, such as 'port' in 'transport' and 'import.'
Define frequent Latin and Greek roots (such as 'aqua,' 'bio,' 'graph,' 'spect') and use them to explain word meanings.
Break unfamiliar words into root, prefix, and suffix to predict their meaning.
Trace the etymology of an English word back through Latin or Greek and explain how its meaning shifted over time.
Use knowledge of Latin and Greek roots to decode specialized academic, scientific, and theological vocabulary.

CFL.3.1.4.t: Arrange words in the right order so that a sentence makes sense.
Explain why changing word order can change or destroy a sentence's meaning.
Identify the parts a complete sentence needs, such as a subject and a verb.
Explain how grammatical rules follow a logic that lets a listener recover the intended meaning.
Analyze how ambiguous sentences arise and how syntax resolves or preserves the ambiguity.
Evaluate why certain grammatical structures are necessary for clear reasoning and valid argument, connecting syntax to logic.

CFL.3.1.5.t: Notice that verbs can tell whether something happens now, happened before, or will happen later.
Identify the tense of an English verb as past, present, or future.
Distinguish when an action is ongoing versus completed (for example, 'was building' versus 'built').
Define grammatical aspect and explain how it differs from tense (time of action versus the way the action unfolds).
Compare how Koine Greek verbs foreground aspect (aorist, present, perfect) while English verbs foreground time.
Analyze a Koine Greek verb's aspect in a passage and explain what nuance it adds beyond an English tense translation.

CFL.3.2.1.t: Break a compound or affixed word into smaller meaningful parts.
Identify a root word and the prefix or suffix added to it.
Explain how adding an affix changes a word's meaning or its part of speech.
Distinguish inflection (changing a word's form for grammar, like plural or past tense) from derivation (making a new word).
Analyze how an inflected language builds many word forms from one root through systematic endings.
Compare morphological strategies across languages, contrasting isolating, agglutinative, and fusional patterns.

CFL.3.2.2.t: Match letters and letter combinations to the sounds they make.
Identify the separate sounds (phonemes) that make up a spoken word.
Distinguish vowels from consonants and describe how each is produced.
Explain how a language's sound system allows only certain sounds and combinations.
Use phonetic symbols to describe how a sound is articulated (place and manner).
Analyze how sounds change in connected speech and across related languages (sound shifts).
Compare the phonological inventories of two languages and explain why some sounds are hard for a foreign speaker to hear or produce.

CFL.3.2.3.t: Notice that the same words can mean different things depending on the situation.
Explain how tone of voice or setting changes what a sentence means.
Identify when a speaker means something other than the literal words (for example, sarcasm or a hint).
Explain how context and shared assumptions let a listener infer a speaker's intended meaning.
Analyze how implication, presupposition, and politeness shape meaning beyond the literal sentence.
Evaluate how cultural and historical context governs the meaning of an utterance, including biblical texts.

CFL.3.2.4.t: Give the meaning of a familiar word.
Identify words that mean the same (synonyms) and words that mean the opposite (antonyms).
Explain how one word can have several related meanings.
Distinguish a word's denotation (dictionary meaning) from its connotation (feeling or association).
Analyze sense relations among words, such as hyponymy, and map how a word's semantic range overlaps with others.
Evaluate how the semantic range of a Hebrew or Greek term shapes translation and interpretation choices.

CFL.3.2.5.t: Notice that people in different places or groups may say the same thing in different ways.
Identify formal versus casual ways of speaking for different situations.
Explain what a dialect is and give examples of regional word or pronunciation differences.
Distinguish register, jargon, and slang, and explain when each is appropriate.
Analyze how social factors such as region, group, and setting shape the way people use language.
Evaluate how a speaker adjusts register and dialect for audience and purpose, and what that signals socially.

CFL.3.2.6.t: Put words in order to build a complete sentence.
Identify the subject and the predicate of a sentence.
Label the main parts of a sentence, including phrases and clauses.
Diagram a sentence to show how its parts relate to one another.
Compare word-order patterns across languages (such as subject-verb-object versus subject-object-verb).
Analyze how a surface sentence can express a deeper underlying structure, and how one meaning yields different arrangements.

CFL.3.3.1.t: Use kind and honest words when speaking to others.
Explain why telling the truth honors God and respects other people.
Identify speech that builds others up versus speech that tears them down.
Choose words that edify and avoid coarse, profane, or deceitful language.
Explain how Scripture calls believers to speak truth in love and to let their speech give grace to hearers.
Evaluate how a Christian's language should reflect truthfulness, charity, and reverence in different settings.

CFL.3.3.2.t: Read simple, familiar texts smoothly and with understanding.
Read comfortable books often to build fluency and enjoyment.
Explain how reading material slightly above one's current level helps language grow.
Apply extensive reading by choosing texts with mostly known words to build fluency in a new language.
Explain the idea of comprehensible input and how it supports acquiring a language.
Design a reading plan that gradually increases difficulty to build fluency in a target language such as Latin or Greek.

CFL.3.3.3.t: Practice new words using picture cards or simple flashcards.
Use flashcards to review vocabulary and check what has been learned.
Practice speaking or writing new words, not just recognizing them.
Explain the difference between input (reading and listening) and output (speaking and writing) in language learning.
Combine flashcards, immersion, and output practice into a balanced study routine.
Evaluate the strengths and limits of each strategy and adjust the balance for a specific learning goal.

CFL.3.3.4.t: Use a simple rhyme or picture to help remember something.
Create a mnemonic, such as a phrase or acronym, to recall a list or rule.
Review material over several days rather than all at once.
Explain how spaced repetition strengthens memory by reviewing at increasing intervals.
Apply spaced repetition and mnemonic techniques to memorize vocabulary or grammar forms.
Explain encoding specificity and design study conditions that match the way information will later be recalled.

CFL.3.3.5.t: Look up a word in a dictionary to find its meaning.
Use alphabetical order and guide words to find an entry quickly.
Read a dictionary entry to find a word's part of speech, meanings, and example uses.
Explain the difference between a bilingual dictionary and a monolingual (same-language) one, and when to use each.
Use a lexicon to look up a Hebrew or Greek word by its root or lemma and read its glosses.
Analyze a lexicon entry to weigh a word's semantic range, cited references, and usage before choosing a meaning in context.

CFL.4.1.1.t: Recognize familiar Latin phrases from Christian worship and Scripture, such as Gloria in excelsis Deo, Pater noster, and Amen
Read aloud short memorized Vulgate verses, such as the Lord's Prayer or Psalm openings, with ecclesiastical pronunciation
Translate simple Vulgate passages using known vocabulary, comparing the Latin wording to a familiar English version
Identify distinctive features of Late and Ecclesiastical Latin, such as simplified word order and Greek loanwords, in Vulgate and patristic texts
Translate and analyze selected passages from the church fathers, such as Augustine's Confessiones or Ambrose's hymns, noting grammar and vocabulary
Read an extended Latin passage from Augustine or Ambrose and discuss how its Latin style conveys theological meaning

CFL.4.1.2.t: Retell key stories of early Rome, such as Romulus and Remus and the founding of the city, and locate Rome on a map
Distinguish the Roman Republic from the Roman Empire and describe how each was governed
Identify major Roman officials and institutions, such as consuls, the Senate, and tribunes, and explain their roles
Describe the careers and significance of key figures such as Julius Caesar, Cicero, and Augustus
Explain foundational concepts of Roman law, such as the Twelve Tables, citizenship, and the ius civile, and their influence on Western legal traditions
Read adapted or original Latin historical prose, such as passages from Caesar or Livy, and analyze how Romans described their own government

CFL.4.1.3.t: Name the major Roman gods and goddesses and describe their chief attributes and domains
Match Roman deities to their Greek counterparts, such as Jupiter/Zeus and Venus/Aphrodite, and note key differences
Retell the deeds of major Roman heroes and legendary figures, such as Aeneas, Hercules, and Romulus
Explain how Roman myths reflected and reinforced Roman values such as pietas, virtus, and civic duty
Summarize the plot and major themes of Virgil's Aeneid and describe its role in Roman national identity
Translate and scan selected passages from Virgil's Aeneid, analyzing imagery, allusion, and poetic technique

CFL.4.2.1.t: Recognize that Latin is read with two main pronunciation systems, Classical and Ecclesiastical
Contrast how key letters and combinations are pronounced in each system, such as c, g, v, ae, and ti
Read the same passage aloud in both Classical and Ecclesiastical pronunciation
Explain the historical and cultural contexts in which each pronunciation system is used and choose the appropriate one for a given text

CFL.4.2.2.t: Recite the Latin alphabet and name the letters that differ in use from English, such as the absence of j and w
Pronounce the Latin vowels with their long and short sounds
Pronounce the Latin diphthongs, such as ae, oe, au, and ei
Pronounce Latin consonants and consonant combinations correctly, noting differences from English
Read aloud unfamiliar Latin words accurately by applying the sounds of vowels, diphthongs, and consonants

CFL.4.2.3.t: Divide Latin words into syllables using vowel and consonant patterns
Determine whether a syllable is long or short by nature or by position
Apply the penultimate rule to place the stress accent correctly in two- and three-syllable words
Explain the difference between the classical quantitative rhythm of Latin and the stress-based accent used in reading, and mark accents in longer words

CFL.4.2.4.t: Learn and use a core set of high-frequency Latin words for everyday nouns, verbs, and adjectives
Identify English words derived from Latin roots and explain their shared meaning
Analyze how common Latin prefixes, such as ad-, con-, in-, and trans-, change the meaning of a base word
Analyze how common Latin suffixes form English derivatives and use them to infer word meanings
Determine the meaning of unfamiliar English and Latin words by breaking them into roots, prefixes, and suffixes

CFL.4.3.1.t: Recognize that a Latin adjective must agree with its noun in gender, number, and case
Decline first- and second-declension adjectives and match them to nouns of each gender
Decline third-declension adjectives and use them with nouns of any declension
Form the comparative and superlative degrees of regular adjectives
Form and translate irregular comparisons, such as bonus, melior, optimus, and use comparison in sentences

CFL.4.3.2.t: Name the six Latin cases and state the basic question each answers
Use the nominative for the subject and the accusative for the direct object in simple sentences
Use the genitive to show possession and the dative to show the indirect object
Identify common uses of the ablative, such as means, manner, and accompaniment
Use the vocative for direct address and recognize special vocative forms
Identify the case and syntactic function of any noun in a Latin sentence and translate it accordingly

CFL.4.3.3.t: Recognize that Latin nouns belong to declensions and that endings signal case and number
Decline first- and second-declension nouns fully in the singular and plural
Decline third-declension nouns, including i-stems, and identify their gender patterns
Decline fourth- and fifth-declension nouns and note their characteristic endings
Determine a noun's declension and gender from its nominative and genitive forms and give the correct stem
Identify and correctly form exceptional and irregular nouns, such as vis, deus, and Greek-declension nouns

CFL.4.3.4.t: Recognize common Latin prepositions and their basic meanings
Use prepositions that take the accusative case, such as ad, per, and trans, in phrases of motion and direction
Use prepositions that take the ablative case, such as in, cum, ab, and de, in phrases of place and separation
Distinguish the difference in meaning when a preposition such as in governs the accusative versus the ablative

CFL.4.3.5.t: Recognize that Latin verbs change endings to show person and number and identify the personal endings
Conjugate first- and second-conjugation verbs in the present tense, active voice
Conjugate third-, third-io, and fourth-conjugation verbs in the present tense
State the four principal parts of a verb and explain what each provides
Conjugate verbs in the imperfect and future tenses across all conjugations
Form the perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect tenses from the perfect stem
Produce and translate complete verb paradigms across all tenses, persons, and numbers

CFL.4.3.6.t: Distinguish between an active verb, whose subject acts, and a passive verb, whose subject is acted upon
Conjugate verbs in the present, imperfect, and future passive using the passive personal endings
Form the perfect passive tenses using the perfect passive participle with forms of sum
Convert sentences between active and passive voice and translate each accurately

CFL.4.4.1.t: Identify subordinate clauses in a Latin sentence and the conjunctions that introduce them
Translate cum clauses expressing time, cause, and circumstance
Recognize and translate purpose clauses introduced by ut and ne with the subjunctive
Recognize and translate result clauses introduced by ut with the subjunctive and distinguish them from purpose clauses

CFL.4.4.2.t: Recognize the subjunctive mood and describe how it differs in function from the indicative
Translate indirect statement expressed with the accusative-plus-infinitive construction
Translate indirect command using ut or ne with the subjunctive after verbs of ordering and asking
Translate indirect question using an interrogative word with the subjunctive and apply the sequence of tenses

CFL.4.4.3.t: Label the subject, verb, and direct object in a simple Latin sentence
Parse a Latin noun or verb by stating all of its grammatical properties, such as case, number, gender, tense, and person
Diagram a Latin sentence to show the relationship between its main and subordinate parts
Parse and diagram a complex Latin sentence to reveal the function of every word and clause

CFL.4.4.4.t: Observe that Latin commonly places the verb at the end of the sentence, unlike English
Translate Latin sentences into natural English word order by reading for endings rather than position
Explain how Latin's inflected endings allow flexible word order without changing basic meaning
Analyze how an author's deliberate placement of words creates emphasis, contrast, or rhetorical effect

CFL.5.1.1.t: Say a simple greeting and your name to introduce yourself to a new friend
Ask and answer basic needs questions such as where the bathroom, food, or water is
Share the gospel message using a memorized set of simple sentences
Pray aloud and lead a short devotional in the target language with a small group
Serve on a service or mission project by interpreting simple conversations between visitors and locals
Explain your beliefs and testimony in extended conversation, responding to questions and objections

CFL.5.1.2.t: Greet a peer and an elder using the correct casual and respectful greetings
Use polite words for please, thank you, and excuse me in everyday interactions
Choose the correct formal or informal form of address based on who you are speaking to
Perform common courtesy gestures correctly and avoid gestures considered rude in the culture
Follow the customs of hospitality, such as greetings at a meal, gift-giving, and table manners
Adjust your tone, address, and body language appropriately across formal, business, and family settings

CFL.5.1.3.t: Name the main countries or regions where the target language is spoken and locate them on a map
Identify the capital cities, major landmarks, and neighboring nations of the target region
Describe key holidays, foods, and everyday customs of the target culture
Summarize major events in the history of the target region and how they shaped the culture
Explain how geography and history have influenced the spread and dialects of the language
Analyze how the region's religious history affects present openness to the gospel and missions

CFL.5.1.4.t: Recognize familiar words and labels in simple picture books and signs in the target language
Read a short, illustrated story aloud and retell its main idea
Read a website page or news headline and identify its topic using context and cognates
Summarize a newspaper or magazine article and explain the author's main point
Read an excerpt of authentic literature and discuss its themes and style
Compare how a current event is reported across target-language and English sources

CFL.5.1.5.t: Notice a word in the target language that has no simple English translation and describe what it means
Explain an idiom or figure of speech and why a word-for-word translation misses its meaning
Describe a cultural value or concept that the language expresses but English does not have a single word for
Explain how a language's structure, such as formality levels or kinship terms, reflects its speakers' worldview
Evaluate how untranslatable concepts create both bridges and barriers when sharing biblical truth

CFL.5.2.1.t: Recognize that some languages change the endings of words to show their role in a sentence
Identify the subject and object of a sentence and the case forms that mark each
Use the correct case forms for subjects, direct objects, and indirect objects in simple sentences
Apply the correct case after common prepositions and possessive constructions
Decline nouns, articles, and adjectives together accurately across the full case system

CFL.5.2.2.t: Say and recognize the most common everyday words for people, objects, colors, and numbers
Use the highest-frequency words for greetings, family, food, and daily activities in sentences
Build a personal vocabulary notebook and review high-frequency words with flashcards
Understand and use common idioms and fixed expressions in everyday conversation
Master the core high-frequency vocabulary that covers most everyday speech and reading
Use idioms, collocations, and topic-specific vocabulary fluently and appropriately in context

CFL.5.2.3.t: Match each noun with its correct article, such as the words for a and the
Identify the gender of common nouns and use the matching article
Make adjectives agree with the noun they describe in gender and number
Apply gender, number, and article agreement correctly throughout a full sentence
Use correct agreement with irregular nouns, plurals, and less common gender patterns

CFL.5.2.4.t: Arrange words in the correct order to make a simple statement
Turn a statement into a question and a negative sentence using correct word order
Identify the basic word-order pattern of the target language, such as subject-verb-object
Build compound sentences using conjunctions while keeping correct word order
Construct complex sentences with subordinate clauses in the correct order
Vary word order for emphasis or style while keeping the sentence grammatical

CFL.5.2.5.t: Use the correct present-tense form of a common verb to match the subject
Conjugate regular verbs in the present tense across all persons and numbers
Speak and write about the past and future using the appropriate verb tenses
Conjugate common irregular verbs correctly across tense, person, and number
Use moods such as the conditional or subjunctive to express possibility, wishes, or commands
Choose and combine tenses and moods accurately to express complex time and meaning

CFL.5.3.1.t: Repeat greetings and simple phrases, imitating the speaker's sounds as closely as you can
Pronounce common words clearly with correct stress and rhythm
Use the rising and falling intonation patterns of the language in questions and statements
Read a short passage aloud with smooth pacing and natural-sounding pronunciation
Speak at length with an accent close enough to a native speaker to be easily understood

CFL.5.3.2.t: Recognize familiar words and follow simple spoken commands and greetings
Understand short, slow sentences about familiar topics and respond appropriately
Follow a simple spoken story or dialogue and answer questions about it
Understand the main idea of speech spoken at a natural pace on familiar topics
Understand extended speech, such as a talk or broadcast, and note its key points
Follow fast, natural conversation including some slang and different accents

CFL.5.3.3.t: Listen for and imitate sounds in the target language that do not exist in English
Place your tongue, lips, and mouth correctly to produce individual target-language sounds
Distinguish and produce pairs of sounds that are easy to confuse
Read and use the phonetic symbols that show how a word is pronounced
Produce difficult sounds and sound combinations accurately in connected speech

CFL.5.3.4.t: Practice a memorized greeting or short exchange with a partner
Act out a simple role-play, such as ordering food or asking directions
Shadow-repeat a recording, matching the speaker's words and rhythm
Hold a short unscripted conversation on a familiar topic with a partner
Improvise dialogue in a role-play that includes an unexpected problem to solve
Sustain an extended spontaneous conversation, expressing and defending your opinions

CFL.5.3.5.t: Recognize and name the letters or characters of the target-language alphabet
Write the letters or characters correctly and match each to its sound
Read and write the diacritical marks or accents that change a letter's sound or meaning
Spell familiar words correctly, including their diacritics
Read and write fluently in the target script, applying its spelling and accent rules

standards: CSTA 3A-AP-14 — Use lists to simplify solutions, generalizing computational problems instead of repeatedly using simple variab (grades 9-10)

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-12 — Compare and contrast fundamental data structures and their uses. Clarification: Examples could include strings (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.2.t: Identify and fix a simple error in an algorithm or program that uses a sequence or a loop

standards: CSTA 1A-AP-14 — Debug (identify and fix) errors in an algorithm or program that includes sequences and simple loops (grades K-2)

CPT.1.1.2.t: Test a program with sample inputs and debug it so it runs as intended

standards: CSTA 1B-AP-15 — Test and debug (identify and fix errors) a program or algorithm to ensure it runs as intended (grades 3-5)

CPT.1.1.2.t: Construct a trace table that records the value of each variable as a program executes step by step

standards: CSTA 1B-AP-15 — Test and debug (identify and fix errors) a program or algorithm to ensure it runs as intended (grades 3-5)

CPT.1.1.2.t: Use a trace table to locate the exact statement where a logic error occurs

standards: CSTA 1B-AP-15 — Test and debug (identify and fix errors) a program or algorithm to ensure it runs as intended (grades 3-5)

CPT.1.1.2.t: Develop a series of test cases to verify a program performs according to its design specification

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-21 — Develop and use a series of test cases to verify that a program performs according to its design specification (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.2.t: Apply a systematic debugging strategy that isolates a fault by narrowing down its cause

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-21 — Develop and use a series of test cases to verify that a program performs according to its design specification (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.3.t: Add input validation that rejects values outside the range a program expects

standards: CSTA 2-AP-17 — Systematically test and refine programs using a range of test cases. Clarification: Use cases and test cases a (grades 6-8)

CPT.1.1.3.t: Test a program deliberately with invalid input such as negative numbers, zero, or wrong data types

standards: CSTA 2-AP-17 — Systematically test and refine programs using a range of test cases. Clarification: Use cases and test cases a (grades 6-8)

CPT.1.1.3.t: Implement error handling that lets a program respond gracefully instead of crashing

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-21 — Develop and use a series of test cases to verify that a program performs according to its design specification (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.3.t: Develop test cases that include boundary and edge conditions to expose weaknesses

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-21 — Develop and use a series of test cases to verify that a program performs according to its design specification (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.3.t: Design a robust program that anticipates and defends against foreseeable user and system errors

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-21 — Develop and use a series of test cases to verify that a program performs according to its design specification (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.4.t: Write a program that reads data from an external text file

standards: CSTA 3A-AP-18 — Create artifacts by using procedures within a program, combinations of data and procedures, or independent but (grades 9-10)

CPT.1.1.4.t: Write a program that saves output by writing data to an external file

standards: CSTA 3A-AP-18 — Create artifacts by using procedures within a program, combinations of data and procedures, or independent but (grades 9-10)

CPT.1.1.4.t: Process the contents of a file line by line to extract or transform information

standards: CSTA 3A-AP-18 — Create artifacts by using procedures within a program, combinations of data and procedures, or independent but (grades 9-10)

CPT.1.1.4.t: Build a program that reads input from one file, processes it, and writes results to another

standards: CSTA 3A-AP-18 — Create artifacts by using procedures within a program, combinations of data and procedures, or independent but (grades 9-10)

CPT.1.1.4.t: Handle file-related errors such as a missing or unreadable file without crashing

standards: CSTA 3A-AP-18 — Create artifacts by using procedures within a program, combinations of data and procedures, or independent but (grades 9-10)

CPT.1.1.5.t: Import an existing library and call its functions inside an original program

standards: CSTA 2-AP-16 — Incorporate existing code, media, and libraries into original programs, and give attribution. Clarification: B (grades 6-8)

CPT.1.1.5.t: Incorporate portions of existing code or media into a program and give proper attribution

standards: CSTA 2-AP-16 — Incorporate existing code, media, and libraries into original programs, and give attribution. Clarification: B (grades 6-8)

CPT.1.1.5.t: Use the functions provided by a library to add capability without rewriting them

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-16 — Demonstrate code reuse by creating programming solutions using libraries and APIs. Clarification: Libraries an (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.5.t: Demonstrate code reuse by building a solution around one or more libraries and APIs

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-16 — Demonstrate code reuse by creating programming solutions using libraries and APIs. Clarification: Libraries an (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.5.t: Connect a program to a web API and use the data it returns

standards: CSTA 3B-AP-16 — Demonstrate code reuse by creating programming solutions using libraries and APIs. Clarification: Libraries an (grades 11-12)

CPT.1.1.6.t: Combine (concatenate) strings and variables to build a message or sentence

standards: CSTA 2-AP-11 — Create clearly named variables that represent different data types and perform operations on their values. Cla (grades 6-8)

CPT.1.1.6.t: Access individual characters and substrings by position within a string

standards: CSTA 2-AP-11 — Create clearly named variables that represent different data types and perform operations on their values. Cla (grades 6-8)

CPT.1.1.6.t: Cast values between strings and numbers so they can be used in the right operations

standards: CSTA 2-AP-11 — Create clearly named variables that represent different data types and perform operations on their values. Cla (grades 6-8)

CPT.1.1.6.t: Use built-in string operations such as length, changing case, replacing, and splitting

Evaluate why the historicity of Adam matters for the Christian doctrines of sin and salvation.

HSS.5.2.2.t: Retell how God created the first people in Genesis 1-2.
Explain what it means that human beings are made in the image of God (imago Dei).
Describe the original righteousness and dignity given to humanity at creation.

Analyze how Marxism's materialist assumptions shape its goals and its view of God.
Evaluate the claims and historical outcomes of Marxism and communism, representing them accurately.

Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of postmodernism and relativism, treating them fairly.
